The "revoke sessions" deny policy
Explicit Deny: it always wins over any Allow.
All actions on all resources.
Targets only tokens issued BEFORE the given date (aws:TokenIssueTime).
Put the date/time of the moment of revocation: new sessions (after) are not blocked by this statement.
Can a temporary session issued at 09:00 (before the date) still call s3:GetObject?
It is denied: TokenIssueTime is earlier than the date, so the Deny applies.
Is a session issued at 11:00, already allowed elsewhere, blocked by this statement?
No: the DateLessThan condition is false for this token, so this statement does not apply.
Can this Deny be bypassed by an Allow * in another policy?
An explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.

How do you handle compromised AWS credentials?

I identify the affected IAM user with GuardDuty. I rotate the exposed credentials: disable then delete the old key. Since temporary credentials may have been issued, I attach an explicit deny policy with an STS date condition. Then I review CloudTrail to detect unauthorized actions, delete the resources created by the attacker, and verify the account information.
Deny + STS date condition
delete unauthorized resources
Why is deleting the access key not enough?

Because temporary credentials obtained with this identity remain valid until they expire. You therefore need a deny policy that refuses any session whose aws:TokenIssueTime is earlier than the time of revocation. New legitimate sessions issued afterward are not affected by this condition.
TokenIssueTime

In addition to rotating the access keys, I rotate and delete unauthorized credentials (IAM user passwords), delete and replace all EC2 Key Pairs, review CloudTrail, delete unauthorized resources, and verify the account information.
